prompt.context: Your client is Amy Sherald, the Chief People Officer at the Metropolitan Museum of Art ('The Met'). Located in New York City, the Met is one of the world's largest art museums with 250 gallery rooms and a collection of more than 2 million works of art. This mega-museum welcomes over 6 million visitors annually. Your client's department reported unusually high human resources (HR) costs last year and has come under scrutiny by the Executive team and Board of Directors. Amy has hired your team to help her address this problem.
prompt.question: How should Amy address the unusually high HR costs at The Met?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current structure of The Met's staff?
clarifying_info.a: There are four main staff departments at the Met: 1) artistic, 2) security, 3) administrative and 4) executive. The artistic staff are salaried and responsible for the art collection. The security staff are hired on a part-time, hourly basis and are responsible for protecting the art 24/7. The administrative staff are salaried and work behind the scenes to ensure museum operations run smoothly. The executive staff are the museum's top leaders and includes C-suite staff.

clarifying_info.q: How does The Met hire staff?
clarifying_info.a: The Met uses a mix of online postings, direct referrals, and occasionally hires an executive search firm. Amy describes the process as sourcing, interviewing, onboarding, retaining then turnover.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have a specific goal?
clarifying_info.a: Not really. For now, the client wants to know where to focus and how to plan for cost reductions in the short term.

clarifying_info.q: How does The Met make money?
clarifying_info.a: The Met is a non-profit and generates revenue from government grants, donations and admission tickets. The client does not want your insight on improving these revenue streams.

exhibits.title: 2019 Museum Department Snapshot
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four departments (Artistic, Executive, Administrative, Security) across five metrics: Cost per Staff Turnover, Average Time-to-fill, Staff Count as of 01/01/2019, % Turnover, and Compensation Type.

framework: Direct Costs: wages and benefits, recruiting (applicant tracking system), training/education, retention/enrichment, turnover/severance packages, overhead and HR team capacity
Indirect Costs: opportunity cost from underperformance of hired staff, loss of knowledge with turnover, decline in morale with turnover or poor management
External Factors: economic cycle, competition, new museum openings, labor force supply vs. demand, education patterns, union considerations
Differentiate by department type (Artistic, Executive, Administrative, Security) — especially salary vs. hourly staff — as cost drivers differ significantly across groups

questions.prompt: How much did turnover cost The Met in 2019? (Note: turnover cost $1.5M in 2018.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should use staff count, % turnover, and cost per staff turnover for each department to calculate total turnover cost. A strong candidate will build a clear department-by-department structure, then sum totals and compare to 2018 baseline (noting ~33-39% increase). Candidate should identify Security as the largest contributor in absolute cost and recommend focusing on that department.

math.setup: For each department: Turnover Count = Staff Count x % Turnover; Turnover Cost = Turnover Count x Cost per Staff Turnover
steps: Year-over-year change: ($2.09M - $1.5M) / $1.5M ≈ 39% increase (or ~33% increase depending on rounding)
math.answer: ~$2.09M total turnover cost in 2019; roughly $600K more than 2018, a ~33-39% increase. Security department alone accounts for ~$1M (almost half of total).

questions.prompt: Does Amy have the optimal number of security staff members? (Optional — use if time allows)
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate the required security staff using the given constraints. A good candidate reaches 1,000 as the optimal number and notes The Met is overstaffed. A great candidate connects the 200-person surplus to the 2019 security turnover count and recommends not replacing those vacant positions in 2020.

math.setup: Museum is open 8 hrs/day (10am-6pm), closed 16 hrs/day. 250 gallery rooms. Staff work max 35 hrs/week = average 5 hrs/day. Calculate staff needed when open and when closed, then convert to FTE headcount.
steps: When open: 2 staff/room x 250 rooms = 500 staff positioned; 500 staff x 8 hrs open = 4,000 security-hours/day needed; 4,000 / 5 hrs per staff per day = 800 FTE equivalent
When closed: 1 staff per 4 rooms = 250/4 = 62.5 staff positioned; 62.5 x 16 hrs closed = 1,000 security-hours/day needed; 1,000 / 5 hrs per staff per day = 200 FTE equivalent
Current staff count = 1,200; Surplus = 1,200 - 1,000 = 200 (which equals the 2019 security turnover count of 200)
math.answer: Optimal security headcount is 1,000. The Met is overstaffed by 200. Since 200 security staff turned over in 2019, Amy could simply not replace those vacancies in 2020 to right-size the department without layoffs.

brainstorming.prompt: Amy wants to explore ways to cut HR costs in the security department overall. Brainstorm some ideas for her.

categories.name: Sourcing
ideas: Cut unnecessary advertising — drop subscriptions to channels that do not generate applications
Optimize screening criteria for faster and more effective candidate filtering
Launch an employee referral program to reduce external search costs

categories.name: Interviewing and Onboarding
ideas: Streamline the applicant tracking system across departments for long-term efficiency
Use first-round phone interviews to reduce time and cost per candidate
Partner with universities and community colleges (security staff credit programs)
Implement online onboarding training (upfront cost but long-term savings and consistency)

categories.name: Retaining and Reducing Turnover
ideas: Let attrition reduce surplus security staff rather than actively replacing vacancies
Reduce security staff per gallery during slower days or off-peak seasons
Eliminate or cap severance; limit overtime pay
Improve management quality and schedule predictability to boost retention
Introduce tiered benefits based on tenure
Offer low-cost staff perks: museum passes, gift store discounts, exclusive exhibition tours, family days, recognition awards
Provide priority consideration for full-time salaried roles (artistic/administrative) as a retention incentive for security staff

categories.name: Structural / Scheduling Levers
ideas: Analyze visitation patterns to right-size staffing by day and time
Consider a flexible or on-call pool to cover peak periods without fixed headcount

recommendation: The Met experienced an approximately 33-39% increase in turnover costs from 2018 to 2019, reaching ~$2.09M. The security department is responsible for nearly half of that total ($1M). I recommend Amy take two immediate actions: (1) reduce minimum security staff per room during low-visitation periods (e.g., weekday mornings) to lower hours-worked costs; (2) do not replace the ~200 security staff who turned over in 2019 — analysis shows The Met only needs 1,000 security staff under current operational requirements, so those vacancies should remain unfilled.
risks: Fewer security staff per gallery could increase exposure to visitor-caused damage or art theft
Reduced staffing may increase workload and stress for remaining security staff, potentially worsening retention and morale
If visitation grows or operational requirements change, the security headcount model would need to be revisited
next_steps: Quantify the precise cost savings at various security staff reduction levels and weigh against potential security and morale risks
Schedule an in-person meeting to prioritize cost-savings options for the Executive team and Board of Directors
Explore low-cost retention perks for security staff to stabilize turnover rate before headcount is reduced
